content.text: Now compress §7 slightly.

input.old_string:
OntoCoDec translates IE ontologies into composable token-level constraints, automatically compiled from ontologies and validated across 3 datasets, 3+ models, and 2 tasks.
LoRA + greedy S1 near-eliminates DR ($<$\,0.1\%) at R-F1 41--47\%; beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violations at 1.54$\times$ latency.
The central insight is that IE type constraints exceed context-free expressiveness (Proposition~1): the semantic layer applies constructive forward masking via a dynamic entity registry, bridging the gap grammar-only enforcement cannot address (3\% vs.\ 94\% DR reduction).
This empirical enabling dependency is scale-sensitive (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}), suggesting grammar-constrained decoding is necessary but increasingly insufficient as models improve.
Extending to global entity-level type consensus during decoding---eliminating CF without beam search overhead---is the primary direction for future work.

% Section 5 — Event Extraction on WikiEvents (compact, inline)
% exp_ids: ee_qwen_wikievents_unconstrained, ee_llama_wikievents_unconstrained,
%          ee_mistral_wikievents_unconstrained, ee_qwen_wikievents_constrained,
%          ee_llama_wikievents_constrained, ee_mistral_wikievents_constrained_v2
% v3 final data confirmed by Director 2026-05-18.

\subsection{Extension to Event Extraction (Preliminary)}
\label{sec:wikievents}

As a preliminary pilot study, we apply OntoCoDec to event extraction (EE) on WikiEvents~\cite{li2021document,lu2021text2event} (56 event types, 80 roles, 27 entity types, 245 constraints; Appendix~\ref{app:wikievents}) without modification.
Violations extend to EV (event vocabulary), RoV (role vocabulary), and AC (argument constraint, analogous to DR).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  Table: WikiEvents three-model comparison (v3 final)
%  exp_ids: ee_{qwen,llama,mistral}_wikievents_{unconstrained,grammar_only,constrained_v3}
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{2.8pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll rrrr rr@{}}
\toprule
& & \multicolumn{4}{c}{\textbf{Violation Rates (\%)}}
& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{F1}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){3-6} \cmidrule(l){7-8}
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Mode}
  & EV\,$\downarrow$ & RoV\,$\downarrow$ & AC & CF
  & Trig.\,$\uparrow$ & Ent.\,$\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Qwen3-8B}
  & Unconstr.\ & 24.0 & 74.9 & 0.3 & 0 & 11.8 & 0 \\
  & Grammar    & \textbf{0} & 76.1 & 8.2 & --- & --- & --- \\
  & S1    & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0} & 2.1 & 21.1 & 13.4 & 14.1 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{\shortstack[l]{Llama\\3.1-8B}}
  & Unconstr.\ & 10.5 & 88.8 & 0.1 & 0 & 5.7 & 0 \\
  & Grammar    & \textbf{0} & 77.0 & 8.8 & --- & --- & --- \\
  & S1    & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0} & 3.8 & 17.2 & 7.5 & 17.6 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{\shortstack[l]{Mistral\\7B}}
  & Unconstr.\ & 37.3 & 63.9 & 0 & 0 & 2.4 & 0 \\
  & Grammar    & \textbf{0} & 64.0 & 13.8 & --- & --- & --- \\
  & S1    & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0} & 1.3 & 14.9 & 3.9 & 11.7 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}%
\caption{WikiEvents EE results. Zero-shot rows (n$=$246): full WikiEvents corpus; fine-tuning (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}, n$=$20): standard 194/20/20 split~\cite{li2021document}.
Violation rates over parsed documents.
\textemdash{} indicates not applicable (grammar-only has no semantic-layer metrics).
F1 $\times$ 100. Fine-tuning results are preliminary given the small test set ($n{=}20$); bootstrap 95\% CIs for argument F1 span approximately $\pm$3--5\,pp.}
\label{tab:wikievents}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Results.}
Unconstrained EE produces extreme vocabulary violations (EV+RoV $>$85\%; Table~\ref{tab:wikievents}), with entity F1\,=\,0 because the parser cannot process off-schema output.
S1 eliminates EV and RoV across all models, which validates the tokenizer-agnostic design across byte-level BPE and SentencePiece.
Grammar-only eliminates EV but leaves RoV at 64--77\% and surfaces latent AC (8--14\%), consistent with DocRED's pattern (\S\ref{sec:docred-results}); S1 drives RoV to 0\%.
Residual AC (1.3--3.8\%) traces to semantically similar types (e.g., SID vs.\ SEN).
CF rises to 15--21\%, exceeding RE levels (10--12\%) because EE's multi-argument structures increase entity reuse across slots.
Post-hoc filtering is impractical ($<$0.5\% arguments retained).
Unlike RE, EE shows measurable F1 gains: entity F1 0\%\,$\to$\,12--18\%, trigger F1 $+$1.5--1.8\,pp.

% exp_ids: p1_ee_ft_qwen_wikievents_r5, p1_ee_ft_llama_wikievents_r5
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning (preliminary, $n{=}20$).}
On the full official test split (20 documents; 194/20/20~\cite{li2021document}), LoRA + S1 eliminates RoV (Qwen 38.31\%\,$\to$\,0\%, Llama 8.8\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and reduces AC to $\leq$0.8\%, with argument F1 within $\pm$1.1\,pp; trigger F1 shifts ($-$5.4/$-$0.6\,pp) have wide CIs consistent with n${=}$20.
CF remains low (0.77--1.18\%); per-document variance is high (Arg-F1 std/mean ${>}$\,0.5), confirming sufficient power to detect violation elimination but not small F1 differences (power analysis in Appendix~\ref{app:power-analysis-full}).

- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

1	% Runtime overhead (inline paragraph, no subsection header to save space)
2	
3	\paragraph{Runtime overhead.}
4	\label{sec:runtime}
5	S1 overhead is $+$13.1\% on SciERC, lower on DocRED due to amortization over longer sequences; under LoRA, $+$10.0\% with 37\% lower absolute latency.
6	Constraint compilation is one-time $<$0.5\,s; scaling benchmarks confirm constant overhead (2--3\%) up to 200 entity types and 1{,}000 relations (Appendix~\ref{app:scalability}).
7	
8	\paragraph{Beam search compatibility.}
9	\label{sec:beam-results}
10	With LoRA, beam search ($k{=}4$)~\cite{anderson2017guided} eliminates all four violation types on both SciERC and DocRED at both 8B and 70B scales (R-F1 43--47; Appendix~\ref{app:beam-search}), yielding two deployment tiers: greedy S1 ($+$10\% latency, DR${<}$0.1\%, CF${\leq}$1.4\%) and beam S1 (1.54$\times$ latency, all violations${\to}$0\%; Table~\ref{tab:beam-latency}).
11	
12	% exp_ids: r16_70b_scierc_zs_s1, r16_70b_docred_zs_s1, 70b_lora_scierc, 70b_lora_docred_200
13	\paragraph{70B-class validation.}
14	\label{sec:70b-results}
15	On Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct (AWQ INT4),\footnote{All 70B experiments use AWQ INT4 quantization; logit-level effects on constraint enforcement are not isolated.} zero-shot S1 eliminates DR on both datasets (SciERC 6.41\%\,$\to$\,0\%, DocRED 14.98\%\,$\to$\,0\%; R-F1 11--13).
16	% exp_ids: r16_70b_scierc_zs_ablation (grammar_only, semantic_only, full_s1)
17	A four-way ablation reveals scale-dependent layer interaction: semantic-only achieves 84\% DR reduction vs.\ 8B's 24\% (Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation}), though grammar remains necessary for RV elimination and CF control (semantic-only CF${=}$76).
18	% exp_ids: eval_70b_lora_scierc_s1_constrained, eval_70b_lora_docred_200_s1_constrained
19	LoRA confirms composability: DR\,$\to$\,0\% on both datasets (R-F1 44.53, 43.95; $|\Delta| \leq 0.20$\,pp; CF 0.18--1.33\%); cross-family generalization at 70B scale remains to be verified.
20	% exp_ids: eval_70b_lora_docred_200_beam4_s1
21	Beam ($k{=}4$) reduces DocRED parse failures (12.5\%\,$\to$\,0.5\%, R-F1 $+$4.19\,pp); SciERC controlled comparison isolates pure beam gain at $+$0.28\,pp (Appendix~\ref{app:70b-ablation}).
22	
23	% exp_ids: trie_qwen_ft_scierc, trie_qwen_zs_scierc, trie_llama_ft_scierc, trie_llama_zs_scierc
24	\paragraph{Comparison with grammar-constrained approaches.}
25	\label{sec:constrained-baselines}
26	Our grammar-only ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation}, row~2) implements the same constraints as GCD~\cite{geng2023gcd} and BoostCD~\cite{boostcd2025}; vLLM \texttt{guided\_json}~\cite{kwon2023vllm} confirms equivalence (DR${=}$15.26\%; GCD-equiv.\ row, Appendix~\ref{app:gcd-comparison}).
27	The ${\sim}$15\% residual DR is the gap our semantic layer addresses (94\% total reduction); trie-only constraints without JSON enforcement yield 9--51\% parse failure (Appendix~\ref{app:trie-baseline}).
28

1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related_work}
3	
4	We provide a detailed survey in Appendix~\ref{app:related_work}; here we position OntoCoDec along three axes.
5	
6	\paragraph{Constrained decoding.}
7	XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar}, Outlines~\cite{willard2023outlines}, SynCode~\cite{ugare2024syncode}, SGLang~\cite{zheng2024sglang}, and related systems~\cite{beurer-kellner2023lmql,park2024grammar,jsonschemabench2025} enforce format validity via CFG-based token masking.
8	NeuroLogic Decoding~\cite{lu2021neurologic} and \citet{huang2024lookahead} enforce constraints via beam-level reranking; OntoCoDec applies per-token masking, avoiding beam-width dependence.
9	PICARD~\cite{scholak2021picard} and \citet{pldi2025_type_constrained_codegen} compile type systems into prefix automata; OntoCoDec applies constructive forward masking via a dynamic entity registry (\S\ref{sec:composition}).
10	DCCD~\cite{dccd2026} and \citet{nguyen2026thinking} decouple reasoning from constrained generation; OntoCoDec enforces schema semantics within a single forward pass.
11	
12	\paragraph{Schema-aware IE.}
13	GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie}, KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}, GUIDEX~\cite{guidex2025}, GenIE~\cite{josifoski2022genie}, TANL~\cite{paolini2021tanl}, REBEL~\cite{cabot2021rebel}, InstructUIE~\cite{wang2023instructuie}, ADELIE~\cite{qi2024adelie}, and others~\cite{fei2022lasuie,wang2022deepstruct,lu2022uie,lou2023usm,zhou2024universalner} encode ontology structure or frame IE as structured generation, though schema compliance gaps persist~\cite{wadhwa2023revisiting}.
14	GoLLIE and KnowCoder embed schema knowledge via code-style prompts (training-time internalization without runtime enforcement); GoLLIE-7B eliminates DR at severe coverage cost (R-F1${=}$0.0, 46\% empty output), while OntoCoDec achieves R-F1${=}$45.47 at DR${=}$0.09\%.
15	
16	\paragraph{Constraint enforcement in IE.}
17	\citet{roth_yih_2004} and \citet{riedel2010modeling} formulated hard type constraints via ILP; post-hoc validation~\cite{khorshidi2025odke,spires_2024,ontologx_2025} detects violations after generation but discards up to 48\% of predictions.
18	EnriCo~\cite{zaratiana2024enrico} uses ASP; IterGen~\cite{ugare2025itergen} backtracks on violations---OntoCoDec uses forward-only masking at $O(|V|)$ per step.

lines: \paragraph{Schema-aware IE.}

GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie}, KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}, GUIDEX~\cite{guidex2025}, GenIE~\cite{josifoski2022genie}, TANL~\cite{paolini2021tanl}, REBEL~\cite{cabot2021rebel}, InstructUIE~\cite{wang2023instructuie}, ADELIE~\cite{qi2024adelie}, and others~\cite{fei2022lasuie,wang2022deepstruct,lu2022uie,lou2023usm,zhou2024universalner} encode ontology structure or frame IE as structured generation, though schema compliance gaps persist~\cite{wadhwa2023revisiting}.

-GoLLIE and KnowCoder embed schema knowledge via code-style prompts (training-time internalization without runtime enforcement); GoLLIE-7B eliminates DR at severe coverage cost (R-F1${=}$0.0, 46\% empty output), while OntoCoDec achieves R-F1${=}$45.47 at DR${=}$0.09\%.

+GoLLIE and KnowCoder embed schema knowledge via code-style prompts (training-time internalization without runtime enforcement); GoLLIE-7B eliminates DR at severe coverage cost (R-F1${=}$0.0, 46\% empty output; confirmed by our reproduction, Appendix~\ref{app:gollie-comparison}), while OntoCoDec achieves R-F1${=}$45.47 at DR${=}$0.09\%.
\paragraph{Constraint enforcement in IE.}

\citet{roth_yih_2004} and \citet{riedel2010modeling} formulated hard type constraints via ILP; post-hoc validation~\cite{khorshidi2025odke,spires_2024,ontologx_2025} detects violations after generation but discards up to 48\% of predictions.

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates correlate with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (R-F1 41--47\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 48\% of predictions including true positives (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with a scale-dependent empirical enabling dependency: at 8B, the semantic layer achieves only 24\% independent DR reduction (near-complete when combined), while at 70B it reaches 84\% independently.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
LoRA + greedy S1 achieves near-complete DR elimination: DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\% at R-F1 41--47\% ($\pm$0.8\,pp, $+$10\% latency); beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types on both RE datasets under fine-tuning (1.54$\times$ latency).
DR enforcement converts ontologically invalid violations to individually valid but type-inconsistent ones (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned); zero-shot DR drops 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with total violations decreasing $\sim$31\% (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}).

We make a systematic engineering contribution with theoretical grounding:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework: we formalize a well-known intuition that cross-field type constraints require runtime state beyond context-free expressiveness (Proposition~1), yielding pair-based sequential enforcement at each level (\S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas of varying restrictiveness with up to 96 relation types.
    \item A comprehensive evaluation across 3 IE datasets, 3 models (8B-class), and 2 tasks, with 70B validation (full SciERC ablation, preliminary DocRED): DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\% at R-F1 41--47\%; zero-shot ablation reveals an empirical enabling dependency (neither layer alone exceeds 24\% DR reduction at 8B; 84\% at 70B; \S\ref{sec:70b-results}); DR enforcement introduces CF as a correctable side effect (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); beam eliminates all violations; a preliminary pilot study on WikiEvents (n${=}$20 test documents) validates event extraction applicability (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
\end{enumerate}

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion

OntoCoDec compiles IE ontologies into composable token-level constraints, validated across 3 datasets, 3+ models, and 2 tasks.
LoRA + greedy S1 near-eliminates DR ($<$\,0.1\%) at R-F1 41--47\%; beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violations at 1.54$\times$ latency.

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates correlate with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (R-F1 41--47\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 48\% of predictions including true positives (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with a scale-dependent empirical enabling dependency: at 8B, the semantic layer achieves only 24\% independent DR reduction (near-complete when combined), while at 70B it reaches 84\% independently.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
LoRA + greedy S1 achieves near-complete DR elimination: DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\% at R-F1 41--47\% ($\pm$0.8\,pp, $+$10\% latency); beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types on both RE datasets under fine-tuning (1.54$\times$ latency).
DR enforcement converts ontologically invalid violations to individually valid but type-inconsistent ones (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned); zero-shot DR drops 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with total violations decreasing $\sim$31\% (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}).

We make a systematic engineering contribution with theoretical grounding:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework: we formalize a well-known intuition that cross-field type constraints require runtime state beyond context-free expressiveness (Proposition~1), yielding pair-based sequential enforcement at each level (\S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas of varying restrictiveness with up to 96 relation types.
    \item A comprehensive evaluation across 3 IE datasets, 3 models (8B-class), and 2 tasks, with 70B validation (full SciERC ablation, preliminary DocRED): DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\% at R-F1 41--47\%; zero-shot ablation reveals an empirical enabling dependency (neither layer alone exceeds 24\% DR reduction at 8B; 84\% at 70B; \S\ref{sec:70b-results}); DR enforcement introduces CF as a correctable side effect (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); beam eliminates all violations; a preliminary pilot study on WikiEvents (n${=}$20 test documents) validates event extraction applicability (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Cross-Dataset Validation on DocRED}
\label{sec:docred-results}

DocRED (96 relations, 14$\times$ SciERC scale) validates the pattern under a larger, more restrictive ontology (Table~\ref{tab:docred-ablation}).
S1 reduces DR from 18.46\% to 10.21\% ($\downarrow$45\%), eliminates RV (29.66\%\,$\to$\,0.03\%) and ET, with R-F1 $+$0.50\,pp ($p < 0.001$).
The lower DR reduction (45\% vs.\ 94\% on SciERC) reflects DocRED's tighter constraints, which trigger more grammar-first fallback (\S\ref{sec:greedy-limitation}).
Grammar-only \emph{increases} DR (18.46\%\,$\to$\,26.17\%) via \textit{latent violation surfacing}: grammar forces OOV$\to$valid relation mapping, exposing type violations previously masked by vocabulary errors---a distinct cross-dataset confirmation of the empirical enabling dependency.
Fine-tuning resolves residual DR entirely (Table~\ref{tab:composability}; residual decomposition in Appendix~\ref{app:residual-dr-analysis}).
